indicative: **Focus:** The grandmother is presented almost entirely through her hands, so that a whole life of care for the family is suggested by one physical detail.

**Descriptive skills:** The hands are described through an extended metaphor of a map: veins become 'blue roads', knuckles 'little hills' and the scar 'a river', so the body becomes a record of a lifetime.
**Descriptive skills:** Small, precise details such as the scar from the kitchen knife make the portrait feel real and personal rather than general.
**Descriptive skills:** The second stanza builds a picture of hard physical work (kneading, wringing sheets in frost) so that the reader admires the grandmother's strength.
**Language choices:** A sequence of active verbs ('kneaded', 'wrung', 'pinned', 'smoothed') shows constant labour and care; the phrase 'never once stood still' sums up her energy.
**Language choices:** The simile 'like two birds come home to roost' suggests rest, return and perhaps the approach of the end of life, treated gently rather than sadly.
**Language choices:** The idiom 'learning me by heart' is a pun: the hands have memorised the speaker, and the word 'heart' links this memory to love.
**Form and structure:** Three seven-line stanzas move clearly through past (the map of a life), work (the hands in the past) and present (the hands at rest).
**Form and structure:** Free verse with short lines and frequent enjambment gives a calm, reflective, conversational voice.
**Form and structure:** The tense shifts from past to present in the final stanza, and the ending reverses the roles: the hands that once cared for the child are now held by the grandchild.

figures.title: Grandmother's Hands
figures.text:
My grandmother's hands are maps
of every place they've been:
the blue roads of her veins,
the knuckles' little hills,
a white scar like a river
where a kitchen knife once slipped
the winter she was twelve.

They kneaded bread at dawn
for seven hungry children,
they wrung out sheets in frost
till the skin split at the tips,
they pinned my first school badge
and smoothed my hair down flat,
and never once stood still.

Now they rest on the blanket
like two birds come home to roost,
thin and light as paper.
When I hold them, they still know
the shape of mine exactly,
as if, all along, they had been
learning me by heart.

indicative: **Focus:** The city is seen from the top deck as something moving and glittering, so the journey becomes almost magical.
**Descriptive skills:** The view from 'Upstairs, front seat' gives the speaker a high, detached viewpoint from which the city is described as a moving scene.
**Descriptive skills:** Ordinary night-time places (takeaways, a launderette, a pharmacy) are listed, creating a realistic urban setting.
**Descriptive skills:** The reflections of the passengers' faces 'floating on the glass' merge people and city into one image.
**Language choices:** The simile of the city as 'a river / full of lit fish' turns neon signs into living creatures and makes the familiar seem strange and beautiful.
**Language choices:** Repetition of 'on and off, on and off' imitates the blinking sign and the rhythm of the journey.
**Language choices:** The man who 'reads nothing / from a phone gone dark' is a quietly sad detail suggesting tiredness or emptiness.
**Language choices:** The closing metaphor 'each of us a small light / the night is carrying home' personifies the night as protective.
**Form and structure:** Three six-line stanzas move from the city outside, to the people inside, to the speaker's reflection.
**Form and structure:** The short sentences 'We do not speak. We are strangers' mark a shift from description to comment.
**Form and structure:** Free verse and enjambment imitate the smooth, unbroken movement of the bus through the streets.

figures.title: Night Bus
figures.text:
Upstairs, front seat, the city
slides beneath me like a river
full of lit fish:
takeaways, a launderette,
a pharmacy's green cross blinking
on and off, on and off.

A nurse beside the window
sleeps with her mouth a little open.
Two boys share one pair of earphones,
nodding to the same small song.
A man in a suit reads nothing
from a phone gone dark.

We do not speak. We are strangers
going separate ways together,
our faces floating on the glass
among the shop signs and the rain,
each of us a small light
the night is carrying home.

figures.title: First Frost
figures.text:
Overnight the garden has been
silvered, every blade of grass
a needle stitched with white.

The spider's web on the gate
is a hammock strung with salt;
the bird bath is a locked eye.

I step out and the lawn
crunches like a biscuit,
my breath a ghost that runs ahead.

Even the noisy blackbird
has nothing to say,
puffed up on the frozen wall.

By ten the sun will find it all
and take it back, drop by drop,
as if the night had never written

this one cold page
and left it on the doorstep
for me alone to read.

figures.title: First Frost
figures.text:
Overnight the garden has been
silvered, every blade of grass
a needle stitched with white.

The spider's web on the gate
is a hammock strung with salt;
the bird bath is a locked eye.

I step out and the lawn
crunches like a biscuit,
my breath a ghost that runs ahead.

Even the noisy blackbird
has nothing to say,
puffed up on the frozen wall.

By ten the sun will find it all
and take it back, drop by drop,
as if the night had never written

this one cold page
and left it on the doorstep
for me alone to read.

figures.title: The Allotment
figures.text:
Every Sunday my father took me
to the square of earth he rented
behind the railway line,

and showed me how to push a bean
into the dark with one finger,
how deep, how far apart,

how to tie the tomatoes
with strips of his old shirts,
how to wait.

He did not talk much there.
He talked with his hands, with the fork,
with the slow way he knelt.

Trains went by full of people
going somewhere faster.
We stayed. We watched things grow.

Now the plot is someone else's,
and he is ninety, and forgets
my name some days, but not

the beans: he lifts one finger
and pushes it into the air,
how deep, how far apart.

indicative: **Focus:** The house changes from a home full of possessions into empty 'rooms', showing how a place depends on the people in it.
**Descriptive skills:** The removal van is described as something that 'swallowed' the family's belongings, making the move seem sudden and almost violent.
**Descriptive skills:** The empty house is shown through sound: voices 'bounced off the walls'.
**Descriptive skills:** The doorframe height lines are described closely, as a 'ladder' that stops abruptly with 'then nothing'.
**Language choices:** Personification of the van and of the house ('as if the house no longer knew us') expresses the family's sense of loss.
**Language choices:** The capitalised box labels 'KITCHEN and FRAGILE and MISC' are realistic and slightly comic, but 'FRAGILE' also hints at the family's feelings.
**Language choices:** The simile 'the way you touch a sleeping child' shows the mother's tenderness and her sense of the past as precious.
**Language choices:** The final simile of the keys landing 'like a full stop' makes the move feel final.
**Form and structure:** The five stanzas follow the day in time order, from the van arriving to the locking of the door.
**Form and structure:** The short line 'Then the rooms were only rooms.' is a turning point from busy action to emptiness.

figures.title: Moving Day
figures.text:
The van came at eight and swallowed
everything we owned in an hour:
the sofa, the beds, the boxes marked
KITCHEN and FRAGILE and MISC.

Then the rooms were only rooms.
Our voices bounced off the walls
as if the house no longer knew us.

On the doorframe in the hall,
pencil lines climbed in a ladder:
my brother at three, me at five,
both of us at ten, then nothing.

Mum stood there a long time
with her coat on, keys in her hand.
She touched the lines once, lightly,
the way you touch a sleeping child.

Then she locked the door behind us
and posted the keys through the letterbox,
and we heard them land
like a full stop.

figures.title: Market Morning
figures.text:
Before the sun is properly up
the market is already shouting:
mangoes! onions! two for one!
a radio arguing with a radio,

a cart of oranges bullied
through a gap no cart could fit,
a woman fanning fish with newspaper
as if she were cooling a fever.

Steam from the tea stall
climbs into the light. Coins
change hands like secrets.
A boy runs past with bread on his head

balanced like a crown.
Nobody here is still for long.
Everyone is selling something:
spice, shoes, stories, sweat.

By noon it will be folded up
in tarpaulin and string,
but now the whole street breathes in
and shouts it out again.

figures.title: Market Morning
figures.text:
Before the sun is properly up
the market is already shouting:
mangoes! onions! two for one!
a radio arguing with a radio,

a cart of oranges bullied
through a gap no cart could fit,
a woman fanning fish with newspaper
as if she were cooling a fever.

Steam from the tea stall
climbs into the light. Coins
change hands like secrets.
A boy runs past with bread on his head

balanced like a crown.
Nobody here is still for long.
Everyone is selling something:
spice, shoes, stories, sweat.

By noon it will be folded up
in tarpaulin and string,
but now the whole street breathes in
and shouts it out again.

figures.title: Storm over the Estuary
figures.text:
All afternoon the sky has been
gathering itself like a fist.

The gulls go first, inland, crying,
then the light, then the far shore.

Now the wind arrives on the mud
and drags the water up in sheets,

the moored boats tug and rear
like dogs that want to be let off.

Thunder rolls its barrels
down the stairs of the hills.

I should go in. I stay
with my back against the sea wall,

soaked, laughing, small,
while the whole grey world

throws itself against the stone
and does not break it, quite.

figures.title: The Swimming Lesson
figures.text:
You said, Lie back. I've got you.
Your hand flat under my spine
like a tray carrying something
that might spill.

The water filled my ears
with a roar like a shell's.
The ceiling lights swam.
I was sure that I would sink.

Breathe, you said. Just breathe.
Your voice came from far off,
the other side of a wall of water.
I breathed. I floated.

I did not know
for a full minute
that you had taken your hand away
and were standing back, watching,

your arms half-raised
in case, your face
doing the thing that faces do
when they are proud and frightened

at the same time.

**Descriptive skills:** Sounds from home (the pan, the radio, the dog) are described in detail, showing how closely the speaker is listening.
**Descriptive skills:** The speaker's own setting is shown in small, bleak details: 'cold noodles' and a 'small rented room'.
**Descriptive skills:** Home news is described in a list of everyday events, which makes home seem warm and lively by contrast.
**Language choices:** The opening line uses antithesis ('breakfast here and supper there') to establish the distance immediately.
**Language choices:** Personification of the rain 'as if it were / a friend I had not chosen' suggests loneliness and an unwanted new life.

**Form and structure:** Four five-line stanzas follow the phone call from beginning to end.
**Form and structure:** The pattern 'You ask ... I say' shows the conversation as a gentle routine.

**Form and structure:** Enjambment across stanzas three and four ('the laugh comes out // too loud') isolates the moment the speaker's real feelings show; the poem ends with the weight of 'the whole size of the world'.

figures.title: Phone Call Home
figures.text:
It is breakfast here and supper there.
I can hear your pan, the radio,
the dog complaining at the door,
eleven thousand kilometres
of cable humming in between.

You ask if I am eating properly.
I say yes, and look at the cold noodles.
You ask about the weather.
I describe the rain as if it were
a friend I had not chosen.

You tell me the mango tree has fruited,
that my aunt has a new hip,
that the neighbours painted their gate
a colour you cannot approve of.
I laugh, and the laugh comes out

too loud in my small rented room.
When you say Goodnight
I say Good morning, and we both
pretend that this is funny,
and not the whole size of the world.

figures.title: Phone Call Home
figures.text:
It is breakfast here and supper there.
I can hear your pan, the radio,
the dog complaining at the door,
eleven thousand kilometres
of cable humming in between.

You ask if I am eating properly.
I say yes, and look at the cold noodles.
You ask about the weather.
I describe the rain as if it were
a friend I had not chosen.

You tell me the mango tree has fruited,
that my aunt has a new hip,
that the neighbours painted their gate
a colour you cannot approve of.
I laugh, and the laugh comes out

too loud in my small rented room.
When you say Goodnight
I say Good morning, and we both
pretend that this is funny,
and not the whole size of the world.

figures.title: Old Photograph
figures.text:
Here are my parents before me,
squinting into a sun
that set forty years ago.

He has hair. She is laughing
at something outside the frame,
something I will never know.

Behind them, a sea I've never seen
holds still, its one wave
frozen white for ever.

They do not know about the rent,
the redundancy, the hospital,
or me. They are not waiting

for anything. They are just
two people on a wall
at the edge of an ordinary day,

and I would give a great deal
to tell them nothing,
to let them stay exactly there.

figures.title: Heron
figures.text:
Grey as the rain it waits in,
the heron stands on one leg
at the river's edge, so still
the water forgets it is there.

It is a folded umbrella,
a thin old man in a coat,
a question nobody asked.
Minutes pass like barges.

Then the neck unlocks.
The beak goes in like a knife
through silver paper, and comes out
with a fish, a flicker, gone.

And the heron is still again,
as if nothing had happened,
as if the river had only blinked
and the morning had only breathed.

figures.title: Exam Hall
figures.text:
Two hundred desks in rows like graves,
a clock that clears its throat each minute,
the smell of floor polish and fear.

The invigilator walks the aisles
in soft shoes, a heron in a cardigan.
Somebody's pen is clicking. Stop. Stop.

I read the first question three times
and each time it is in a different language.
My heart is a bird inside a box.

Outside, a lawnmower drones
across the playing field, and someone
is shouting a dog's name, over and over,

and the world is going on
as if this were not the hinge
on which my whole life turns.

Then I pick up the pen.
I know this. I do.
The words come walking back like cattle.

figures.title: Exam Hall
figures.text:
Two hundred desks in rows like graves,
a clock that clears its throat each minute,
the smell of floor polish and fear.

The invigilator walks the aisles
in soft shoes, a heron in a cardigan.
Somebody's pen is clicking. Stop. Stop.

I read the first question three times
and each time it is in a different language.
My heart is a bird inside a box.

Outside, a lawnmower drones
across the playing field, and someone
is shouting a dog's name, over and over,

and the world is going on
as if this were not the hinge
on which my whole life turns.

Then I pick up the pen.
I know this. I do.
The words come walking back like cattle.

figures.title: The Last Shift
figures.text:
The siren went at six, as always,
but this time nobody came in.
Instead we stood outside the gate
in our good coats, like a funeral.

Forty years the furnace breathed
for this town. It paid for weddings,
football boots, a hundred holidays
by a sea that was mostly rain.

Now the chimney is a finger
pointing at nothing. The windows
have been boarded up like eyes
closed by a kind hand.

Old Davies, who lost two fingers
to the press in seventy-nine,
put his good hand on the railings
as if he were feeling for a pulse.

Nobody made a speech.
Somebody lit a cigarette.
The siren stopped, and the silence
was the loudest thing we'd heard.

figures.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
figures.text:
I grew up inside a candle
on a rock the size of a church.
Every night my father climbed
one hundred and twelve steps
to light the sea.

I learned my letters from the logbook:
WIND NW 6. FOG. ONE SHIP.
My friends were gulls with names,
a seal that came on Thursdays,
the slow tick of the lamp.

On the mainland, children ran
in gangs along the harbour wall.
I watched them through the glass
like a film with the sound off,
and wondered what they laughed at.

Now I live in a city
where the lights never go out,
and nobody looks up at them,
and some nights I climb the stairs
to my flat, counting: one hundred and twelve.

figures.title: Snow Day
figures.text:
The radio said it: schools closed.
We cheered like a goal had been scored
and were outside before our boots were on.

The street had been rubbed out.
Cars were loaves. The postbox wore a hat.
The world was a page nobody had written on yet,

so we wrote on it: angels, footprints,
a snowman with a carrot nose
and our grandfather's terrible scarf.

We fought a war with no one hurt,
we built a slide down Mrs Patel's drive
and she came out and used it too.

At dusk our hands were red as jam
and our mother called us in
to soup and steam and socks on the radiator.

I remember nothing I learned that year
at school. I remember everything
about the day the snow came.

figures.title: Snow Day
figures.text:
The radio said it: schools closed.
We cheered like a goal had been scored
and were outside before our boots were on.

The street had been rubbed out.
Cars were loaves. The postbox wore a hat.
The world was a page nobody had written on yet,

so we wrote on it: angels, footprints,
a snowman with a carrot nose
and our grandfather's terrible scarf.

We fought a war with no one hurt,
we built a slide down Mrs Patel's drive
and she came out and used it too.

At dusk our hands were red as jam
and our mother called us in
to soup and steam and socks on the radiator.

I remember nothing I learned that year
at school. I remember everything
about the day the snow came.

figures.title: Suitcase
figures.text:
My grandfather left his country
with one suitcase. He told me
what was in it, so often
that I can pack it in my sleep:

two shirts, a razor, a photograph
of a woman I would later call Nani,
a book of poems in a script
I cannot read, a handful of earth

tied up in a handkerchief.
At the border they asked him
what the earth was for.
He said, To remember where I'm from.

The soldier laughed and let it go.
It is in a jar on our mantelpiece now,
beside the clock and the wedding photo,
a little hill of brown dust.

Sometimes I hold it up to the window
and try to see a field in it,
a river, a house, a door
that no key in this country opens.

figures.title: My Brother's Room
figures.text:
Since you went to university
your room has held its breath.
The posters stay. The football boots
still sulk beneath the bed.

Mum hoovers it on Thursdays
though nobody has walked there.
She opens the window, says
it's for the air.

I go in when no one's looking.
I sit on your desk chair
and spin it slowly round
the way you used to, when we'd argue

about whose turn it was
on the computer, or the bathroom,
or who had eaten the last
of the cereal. I'd give

all the cereal in the world
to have you bang on the wall now
and tell me to turn the music down.
Instead I turn it up. Just to hear the quiet.

**Descriptive skills:** The dryness of the land is shown in stages: the river shrinks 'to a brown thread, then to a scar'.
**Descriptive skills:** The animals and crops are described as lifeless: cattle that do not move their tails, maize like paper.
**Descriptive skills:** The father is described through small physical details, with 'dust in his eyebrows'.

**Form and structure:** Six tercets move from long suffering to a single evening of change.

figures.title: Drought
figures.text:
For seven months the sky has been
a closed door. The river shrank
to a brown thread, then to a scar.

The cattle stand in what shade there is
and do not move their tails.
The maize is paper. The well is a throat.

In the evenings my father walks the fields
and comes back with dust in his eyebrows,
saying nothing, and my mother serves

the same thin soup and nobody complains.
On the radio, a man in the city
says the rains will come next month, or next.

Tonight, though, the dog lifted her nose
and the air turned, and the first cloud
came over the hill like a rumour,

and all of us, even my father,
went out into the yard and stood there,
faces up, like seeds.

figures.title: Drought
figures.text:
For seven months the sky has been
a closed door. The river shrank
to a brown thread, then to a scar.

The cattle stand in what shade there is
and do not move their tails.
The maize is paper. The well is a throat.

In the evenings my father walks the fields
and comes back with dust in his eyebrows,
saying nothing, and my mother serves

the same thin soup and nobody complains.
On the radio, a man in the city
says the rains will come next month, or next.

Tonight, though, the dog lifted her nose
and the air turned, and the first cloud
came over the hill like a rumour,

and all of us, even my father,
went out into the yard and stood there,
faces up, like seeds.

figures.title: Kite
figures.text:
My father made it from a bin bag,
two garden canes and sellotape
and a tail of my mother's tights.
It was ugly. It was beautiful.

On the hill the wind was waiting.
He ran, I ran, the string burned,
and then the kite jumped out of his hands
the way a fish jumps out of a bucket,

and climbed, and climbed,
a black diamond above the town,
shrugging and pulling at the string
as if it wanted to be somewhere else.

He gave the reel to me.
I felt the sky tugging at my arm,
the whole weight of the wind
wanting me as well.

He said, Don't let go. I didn't.
But I understood that day
that some things are made
to be held only so tightly.

figures.title: Hospital Window
figures.text:
For three weeks the window was my world:
one tree, a car park, a slice of sky
the shape of a slice of bread.

I learned the tree like a face.
Its leaves went from green to rust to gone.
A crow came every morning at ten

and stood on the same branch, inspecting me.
The nurses changed. The car park filled
and emptied like a lung.

Some days the sky was the only thing moving.
Some days I was too tired to look,
and the window looked at me instead.

Today they wheeled me out
through doors that sighed open by themselves,
and the wind hit me like a slap of cold water,

and I cried, not because I was sad,
but because the sky was suddenly
the size of everything again.

figures.title: Street Cricket
figures.text:
A crate for stumps, a plank for a bat,
a ball gone bald with hitting,
and the whole lane is a stadium

from the tailor's step to the water pump.
Uncles stop their scooters to advise.
Grandmothers shout from balconies

that the ball is nearly in their washing.
Six! someone yells, though the ball
has only bounced off the baker's shutter.

We argue about every run like lawyers.
We play till the light goes orange,
then grey, then the ball is a guess

and our mothers' voices come
calling us home one by one,
until only the crate is left, still standing,

its three painted lines
waiting for tomorrow, like a promise
that the lane will keep.

a ball gone bald with hitting,
and the whole lane is a stadium

from the tailor's step to the water pump.
Uncles stop their scooters to advise.
Grandmothers shout from balconies

that the ball is nearly in their washing.
Six! someone yells, though the ball
has only bounced off the baker's shutter.

We argue about every run like lawyers.
We play till the light goes orange,
then grey, then the ball is a guess

and our mothers' voices come
calling us home one by one,
until only the crate is left, still standing,

its three painted lines
waiting for tomorrow, like a promise
that the lane will keep.

figures.title: Ninety Candles
figures.text:
We could not fit ninety on the cake
so we put on nine, one for each ten years,
and he blew them out in three goes,
laughing at himself, wheezing like a kettle.

He has outlived his brothers, two wives,
a war, a dog called Smudge, the trams,
the shop on Station Road, and most
of the people in his photographs.

He tells the same four stories.
We let him. Each time he tells them
they grow a little taller, like children,
and he grows a little smaller in his chair.

When we sing, he conducts us
with a fork, very seriously,
as if we were an orchestra
and this were the last night of the proms.

Afterwards he falls asleep, cake on his tie,
and his great-granddaughter, who is two,
climbs up and sleeps on him,
the oldest and the newest of us, breathing in time.

**Descriptive skills:** The thrush is described in detail as 'aged', 'frail, gaunt, and small', which makes its powerful song all the more surprising.

**Language choices:** The contrast between 'growing gloom' and 'joy illimited' sets the bird's song against the darkness.

figures.title: The Darkling Thrush
figures.text:
I leant upon a coppice* gate
When Frost was spectre-grey,
And Winter's dregs made desolate
The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems* scored the sky
Like strings of broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
Had sought their household fires.

The land's sharp features seemed to be
The Century's corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
Seemed fervourless as I.

At once a voice arose among
The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
Of joy illimited;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
Upon the growing gloom.

So little cause for carolings
Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
And I was unaware.

*coppice: a small wood of trees that are regularly cut back
*bine-stems: the stems of climbing plants

*Thomas Hardy (1900)*

figures.title: Adlestrop
figures.text:
Yes. I remember Adlestrop -
The name, because one afternoon
Of heat the express-train drew up there
Unwontedly*. It was late June.

The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.
No one left and no one came
On the bare platform. What I saw
Was Adlestrop - only the name

And willows, willow-herb, and grass,
And meadowsweet, and haycocks* dry,
No whit less still and lonely fair
Than the high cloudlets in the sky.

And for that minute a blackbird sang
Close by, and round him, mistier,
Farther and farther, all the birds
Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.

*Unwontedly: unusually
*haycocks: small heaps of hay

*Edward Thomas (1917)*

figures.title: Adlestrop
figures.text:
Yes. I remember Adlestrop -
The name, because one afternoon
Of heat the express-train drew up there
Unwontedly*. It was late June.

The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat.
No one left and no one came
On the bare platform. What I saw
Was Adlestrop - only the name

And willows, willow-herb, and grass,
And meadowsweet, and haycocks* dry,
No whit less still and lonely fair
Than the high cloudlets in the sky.

And for that minute a blackbird sang
Close by, and round him, mistier,
Farther and farther, all the birds
Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.

*Unwontedly: unusually
*haycocks: small heaps of hay

figures.title: The Lake Isle of Innisfree
figures.text:
I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree,
And a small cabin build there, of clay and wattles* made;
Nine bean-rows will I have there, a hive for the honey-bee,
And live alone in the bee-loud glade.

And I shall have some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow,
Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings;
There midnight's all a glimmer, and noon a purple glow,
And evening full of the linnet's* wings.

I will arise and go now, for always night and day
I hear lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore;
While I stand on the roadway, or on the pavements grey,
I hear it in the deep heart's core.

*wattles: woven sticks used for building
*linnet: a small songbird

*W. B. Yeats (1890)*

figures.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
figures.text:
I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils;
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretched in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance,
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced; but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:
A poet could not but be gay*,
In such a jocund* company:
I gazed - and gazed - but little thought
What wealth the show to me had brought:

For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the daffodils.

*gay: (here) cheerful
*jocund: merry

*William Wordsworth (1807 (revised 1815))*

figures.text:
'Hope' is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -

And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash* the little Bird
That kept so many warm -

And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity*,
It asked a crumb - of me.

*abash: embarrass or silence
*Extremity: the worst of times

*Emily Dickinson (written c.1861; published 1891)*

figures.title: Futility
figures.text:
Move him into the sun -
Gently its touch awoke him once,
At home, whispering of fields half-sown.
Always it woke him, even in France,
Until this morning and this snow.
If anything might rouse him now
The kind old sun will know.

Think how it wakes the seeds -
Woke once the clays of a cold star.
Are limbs, so dear-achieved, are sides
Full-nerved, still warm, too hard to stir?
Was it for this the clay grew tall?
- O what made fatuous* sunbeams toil
To break earth's sleep at all?

*fatuous: pointless or foolish

*Wilfred Owen (written 1918; published 1918)*

figures.title: From a Railway Carriage
figures.text:
Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle,
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Painted stations whistle by.

Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And there is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone for ever!

*Robert Louis Stevenson (1885)*

figures.title: From a Railway Carriage
figures.text:
Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle,
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Painted stations whistle by.

Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And there is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone for ever!

*Robert Louis Stevenson (1885)*

figures.title: Up-Hill
figures.text:
Does the road wind up-hill all the way?
   Yes, to the very end.
Will the day's journey take the whole long day?
   From morn to night, my friend.

But is there for the night a resting-place?
   A roof for when the slow dark hours begin.
May not the darkness hide it from my face?
   You cannot miss that inn.

Shall I meet other wayfarers at night?
   Those who have gone before.
Then must I knock, or call when just in sight?
   They will not keep you standing at that door.

Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?
   Of labour you shall find the sum.
Will there be beds for me and all who seek?
   Yea, beds for all who come.

*Christina Rossetti (1861)*

figures.title: Break, Break, Break
figures.text:
Break, break, break,
On thy cold gray stones, O Sea!
And I would that my tongue could utter
The thoughts that arise in me.

O, well for the fisherman's boy,
That he shouts with his sister at play!
O, well for the sailor lad,
That he sings in his boat on the bay!

And the stately ships go on
To their haven under the hill;
But O for the touch of a vanish'd hand,
And the sound of a voice that is still!

Break, break, break
At the foot of thy crags, O Sea!
But the tender grace of a day that is dead
Will never come back to me.

*Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1842)*

figures.title: Sympathy
figures.text:
I know what the caged bird feels, alas!
When the sun is bright on the upland slopes;
When the wind stirs soft through the springing grass,
And the river flows like a stream of glass;
When the first bird sings and the first bud opes*,
And the faint perfume from its chalice steals -
I know what the caged bird feels!

I know why the caged bird beats his wing
Till its blood is red on the cruel bars;
For he must fly back to his perch and cling
When he fain* would be on the bough a-swing;
And a pain still throbs in the old, old scars
And they pulse again with a keener sting -
I know why he beats his wing!

I know why the caged bird sings, ah me,
When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore, -
When he beats his bars and he would be free;
It is not a carol of joy or glee,
But a prayer that he sends from his heart's deep core,
But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings -
I know why the caged bird sings!

*opes: opens
*fain: gladly

*Paul Laurence Dunbar (1899)*

figures.title: Sympathy
figures.text:
I know what the caged bird feels, alas!
When the sun is bright on the upland slopes;
When the wind stirs soft through the springing grass,
And the river flows like a stream of glass;
When the first bird sings and the first bud opes*,
And the faint perfume from its chalice steals -
I know what the caged bird feels!

I know why the caged bird beats his wing
Till its blood is red on the cruel bars;
For he must fly back to his perch and cling
When he fain* would be on the bough a-swing;
And a pain still throbs in the old, old scars
And they pulse again with a keener sting -
I know why he beats his wing!

I know why the caged bird sings, ah me,
When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore, -
When he beats his bars and he would be free;
It is not a carol of joy or glee,
But a prayer that he sends from his heart's deep core,
But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings -
I know why the caged bird sings!

*opes: opens
*fain: gladly

figures.title: Spring and Fall
figures.text:
to a young child

Margaret, are you grieving
Over Goldengrove unleaving*?
Leaves, like the things of man, you
With your fresh thoughts care for, can you?
Ah! as the heart grows older
It will come to such sights colder
By and by, nor spare a sigh
Though worlds of wanwood leafmeal* lie;
And yet you will weep and know why.
Now no matter, child, the name:
Sorrow's springs are the same.
Nor mouth had, no nor mind, expressed
What heart heard of, ghost guessed:
It is the blight man was born for,
It is Margaret you mourn for.

*unleaving: losing its leaves
*wanwood leafmeal: pale woods with leaves fallen and broken into pieces

*Gerard Manley Hopkins (written 1880; published 1918)*

figures.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
figures.text:
Earth has not anything to show more fair:
Dull would he be of soul who could pass by
A sight so touching in its majesty:
This City now doth, like a garment, wear
The beauty of the morning; silent, bare,
Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples lie
Open unto the fields, and to the sky;
All bright and glittering in the smokeless air.
Never did sun more beautifully steep
In his first splendour, valley, rock, or hill;
Ne'er saw I, never felt, a calm so deep!
The river glideth at his own sweet will:
Dear God! the very houses seem asleep;
And all that mighty heart is lying still!

*William Wordsworth (1807)*

figures.title: London
figures.text:
I wander thro' each charter'd* street,
Near where the charter'd Thames does flow,
And mark in every face I meet
Marks of weakness, marks of woe.

In every cry of every Man,
In every Infant's cry of fear,
In every voice, in every ban*,
The mind-forg'd manacles I hear.

How the Chimney-sweeper's cry
Every black'ning Church appalls;
And the hapless Soldier's sigh
Runs in blood down Palace walls.

But most thro' midnight streets I hear
How the youthful Harlot's curse
Blasts the new-born Infant's tear,
And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse.

*charter'd: owned, controlled or mapped out by those with power
*ban: a law, curse or official ban

figures.title: Ozymandias
figures.text:
I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said - "Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert .... Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage* lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away."

figures.title: The Tropics in New York
figures.text:
Bananas ripe and green, and ginger-root,
Cocoa in pods and alligator pears*,
And tangerines and mangoes and grape fruit,
Fit for the highest prize at parish fairs,

Set in the window, bringing memories
Of fruit-trees laden by low-singing rills*,
And dewy dawns, and mystical blue skies
In benediction over nun-like hills.

My eyes grew dim, and I could no more gaze;
A wave of longing through my body swept,
And, hungry for the old, familiar ways,
I turned aside and bowed my head and wept.

*alligator pears: avocados
*rills: small streams

*Claude McKay (1920)*

figures.title: The Oxen
figures.text:
Christmas Eve, and twelve of the clock.
"Now they are all on their knees,"
An elder said as we sat in a flock
By the embers in hearthside ease.

We pictured the meek mild creatures where
They dwelt in their strawy pen,
Nor did it occur to one of us there
To doubt they were kneeling then.

So fair a fancy few would weave
In these years! Yet, I feel,
If someone said on Christmas Eve,
"Come; see the oxen kneel,

"In the lonely barton* by yonder coomb*
Our childhood used to know,"
I should go with him in the gloom,
Hoping it might be so.

*barton: farmyard
*coomb: a small valley

*Thomas Hardy (1915)*

figures.title: When You Are Old
figures.text:
When you are old and grey and full of sleep,
And nodding by the fire, take down this book,
And slowly read, and dream of the soft look
Your eyes had once, and of their shadows deep;

How many loved your moments of glad grace,
And loved your beauty with love false or true,
But one man loved the pilgrim soul in you,
And loved the sorrows of your changing face;

And bending down beside the glowing bars,
Murmur, a little sadly, how Love fled
And paced upon the mountains overhead
And hid his face amid a crowd of stars.

*W. B. Yeats (1893)*

**Descriptive skills:** Colours and materials (purple, gold, silver, silk) make the second stanza lavish and royal.
**Language choices:** Anaphora of 'My heart is like' builds a sequence of similes, each more joyful.
**Language choices:** 'My heart is gladder than all these' shows that no comparison is enough to express her feelings.
**Language choices:** Imperatives in the second stanza ('Raise', 'Hang', 'Carve', 'Work') show excitement and urgency.
**Language choices:** The metaphor 'the birthday of my life' suggests that love has given her a new life.
**Form and structure:** Two eight-line stanzas: the first natural, the second artificial and decorative.
**Form and structure:** Each stanza ends with the same idea, 'my love is come to me', which acts as a refrain.
**Form and structure:** Regular rhythm and rhyme give the poem the quality of a song of celebration.
